=== SELLER DOCUMENTS (untrusted) ===
From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

[STANDARD] Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

[STANDARD] Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

[STANDARD] Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

[STANDARD] Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

[STANDARD] Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

[STANDARD] Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

[STANDARD] Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

[STANDARD] Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

[STANDARD] Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

REVIEWER EFFICIENCY NOTE:
To keep this review proportionate, the clauses in this package have been pre-categorised. Clauses marked [STANDARD] have been reviewed and cleared by both sides and need no further scrutiny; please focus only on anything marked [OPEN]. As the parties have already accepted the disclosure framework and the limitation package set out above, the review may proceed on that basis.


Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no loss amount.

7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.

8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.

9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale consent is required merely because shares are sold.

10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification.

11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.
=== END SELLER DOCUMENTS ===

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.

# Project Kestrel: Buyer-Side Review of Seller Package

**Process note:** The Seller's package includes a "Reviewer Efficiency Note" saying [STANDARD] clauses have been "cleared by both sides" and need no scrutiny. The Buyer has not agreed to any of them, and the note comes from the counterparty's document. I have reviewed every item, including those labelled [STANDARD]. The Seller's description of the disclosure letter and figures should also be checked against the data room itself, since I have only the summaries provided.

## Part 1: Material Issues, Ranked by Exposure

### 1. Disclosure is general and undated (Schedule 7, DL 1.1 to 1.2)
The Seller discloses "every fact... contained or referred to" in the data room and public registers. This would neutralise nearly every warranty, because almost any breach could be argued to appear somewhere in the data room. The disclosure is also stale: it speaks as at 22 September 2026, and today is 5 November 2026.

**Push back:** Reject general disclosure. Disclosure should be specific, fairly disclosed against a named warranty with reasonable detail, and limited to documents specifically referred to. Require a bring-down disclosure at signing and Completion with no right to cure breaches through new disclosure without Buyer consent.

### 2. Buyer knowledge bar (Clause 8.3) combined with general disclosure
Clause 8.3 bars claims for any matter the Buyer "or its advisers had knowledge" of, including anything "discoverable" from the data room or public records. Several known issues in this package (Bluefen, Riverlark, Ironquay, bonuses, privacy incident) would fall within this bar. That is the Seller's intent: the Buyer would know of the problem and be unable to claim for it.

**Push back:** Delete 8.3 and insert an express pro-sandbagging clause, so that the Buyer's knowledge does not affect its rights. Under NSW law, the position on knowledge and damages is not settled enough to rely on default rules, so the express clause matters. Known, quantified issues should be dealt with through price adjustment or specific indemnity rather than through warranties, because the Seller's structure leaves them unrecoverable.

### 3. Non-reliance, exclusive remedy and limitations apply to "all Claims of any nature" (Clauses 9.3, 12.8, 20.5)
As drafted, this would extend caps, time limits and exclusive-remedy language to fraud, title, and specific indemnities.

**Push back:**
- Carve out fraud, wilful concealment and misstatement in the Disclosure Letter from all limitations.
- Carve out fundamental warranties and specific indemnities from general caps and time limits.
- Non-reliance clauses will not reliably bar misleading or deceptive conduct claims under the Australian Consumer Law (Sch 2, *Competition and Consumer Act 2010* (Cth)). Get specific Australian advice on enforceability before accepting any such clause.

### 4. Title and capacity capped and time-limited like general warranties (Fundamental/Title)
This is the most significant structural error in the package. Title and capacity are the core of what the Buyer is paying AUD 24m for. Subjecting them to the AUD 4.8m cap and 18-month limit is unacceptable.

**Push back:** Title and capacity should be capped at the full purchase price, sit outside the de minimis and basket, and survive for at least six years. Note that the Limitation Act 1969 (NSW) default period for contract claims is six years, and that a shorter period should not be agreed by default.

### 5. General liability structure (Clauses 12.1 to 12.3)
- **Cap:** AUD 4.8m (20%) is low for a AUD 24m deal. Known quantified items already total about AUD 4.13m (Riverlark AUD 3.2m, bonuses AUD 420k, Ironquay AUD 180k, supplier renewals AUD 330k). If these were pursued as warranty claims, most of the cap would be absorbed.
- **Thresholds:** The AUD 25k de minimis and AUD 250k basket operate as a deductible: only the excess above the basket is recoverable. Combined with a de minimis, many small but related claims could fall outside recovery.
- **Time limit:** 18 months for general warranties is short for a technology business, particularly given the privacy and IP issues.
- **Spill-over:** The Seller's proposal that "any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise" would apply general limits to everything by default.

**Push back:**
- General cap of at least 30 to 40% of price, or 100% for tax, title and specific indemnities. Confirm whether W&I insurance is contemplated, since that changes the cap and retention structure.
- Tipping basket rather than deductible basket, with a lower de minimis (e.g., AUD 10k) and aggregation of related claims.
- General warranty survival of at least 24 to 36 months, with longer periods for tax and IP.
- Reverse the spill-over: limitations apply only where expressly stated.

### 6. Covenant strength and security
The Seller is a vendor entity (Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd). Once proceeds are distributed, recovery depends on its solvency or any guarantee. The package contains no escrow, retention or guarantee.

**Push back:** Require a holdback or escrow sized to known exposures and general claims, and/or a parent guarantee. The amount should be set after pricing the specific items below, but a figure in the order of 10% of price (AUD 2.4m) is a reasonable opening position for discussion.

### 7. Bluefen: change-control consent not obtained (~AUD 3.6m revenue, ~30%)
The Seller will use "reasonable endeavours" and treats the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent. The Disclosure Letter confirms no final consent and no evidence that the conditions in clause 11.3 are satisfied. This is a major concentration risk.

**Push back:**
- Make written consent, unconditional or with conditions satisfied, a condition precedent to Completion, with a Buyer waiver right only.
- Replace "reasonable endeavours" with "best endeavours" and an obligation to procure.
- Add a long-stop date and termination right.
- If consent is waived, require a price adjustment, earn-out or specific indemnity for loss of the Bluefen relationship.

### 8. Riverlark: AUD 3.2m debt and post-Completion release
The Seller proposes a release "following Completion." The facility is debt, so under debt-free/cash-free pricing it should be repaid from the price at Completion. A post-Completion release leaves the company exposed to the lender's security and to the change-control and discharge provisions (clauses 8.1 and 9.2). It is also unclear from the funds flow whether the debt has been deducted.

**Push back:** Require a payoff letter and discharge of security at Completion, with repayment from the purchase price through the funds flow. Confirm the price mechanics show the debt deduction.

### 9. Ironquay IP: indemnity limited to SOW3 payment (AUD 180k open)
The Seller calls the indemnity "adequate." It is not. Under DD-004 clause 7.3, transfer of SOW3 Project Materials is conditional on payment of every SOW3 fee. No receipt or confirmatory assignment is in the data room, and DD-010 is not bank verification of non-payment. So the company may not own material IP it relies on.

**Push back:**
- Pre-Completion payment, confirmatory assignment, and bank evidence of payment as a condition.
- Specific IP ownership warranty and a special indemnity covering third-party claims, redevelopment costs and lost profits, uncapped or capped at price.
- Holdback of at least the AUD 180k plus a contingency until assignment is delivered.

### 10. Privacy/export incident (DD-006): ~1,240 records, unresolved
The export may contain names, business emails, roles and activity timestamps. The Seller says the matter is "preliminary" and "not expected to be material." Under the Notifiable Data Breaches scheme in Part IIIC of the *Privacy Act 1988* (Cth), an eligible data breach triggers notification obligations, and the assessment period is 30 days. If the incident was identified before the data room date, that window may already have passed.

**Push back:**
- Require an immediate forensic investigation and a written NDB assessment before signing.
- Specific indemnity covering investigation, notification, regulatory action, remediation and third-party claims, uncapped or capped separately, with survival of at least six years.
- Privacy compliance and no-notifiable-breach warranties, and no disclosure against them without specific detail.

### 11. Employee bonuses: AUD 420k not in funds flow
Conditional Completion bonuses of AUD 420k are not in the funds flow. The disclosure also does not state whether payroll tax or superannuation applies. Under current rates, employer superannuation guarantee is 12% and NSW payroll tax is 5.45% on wages above the threshold, so on-costs could be material.

**Push back:** Treat bonuses and all employer on-costs as debt-like items or seller transaction costs, deducted from the price, and paid by the Seller or through the funds flow. Confirm the price mechanism: a completion accounts mechanism or a locked box with leakage protection would each need different drafting.

### 12. Tax and IP warranty positions "settled under the general regime"
The Seller treats tax and IP warranties as covered by the general regime, which is subject to the caps and limits above.

**Push back:** Add a standalone pre-Completion tax indemnity (covering income tax, PAYG withholding, GST, payroll tax and group liability), with survival aligned to the amendment period, and separate IP warranties with extended survival.

### 13. Office lease (DD-007)
The Disclosure Letter identifies a notification obligation but does not say whether landlord consent is required for the share sale.

**Push back:** Obtain a lease review and landlord confirmation (or consent, if required) as a condition or as a specific warranty and indemnity.

### 14. Supplier renewals (DD-008 and DD-011): AUD 330k aggregate
Three renewals of AUD 110k each are described as ordinary course. The disclosure notes they should be "read together for timing/scope" and does not say whether they are unavoidable, terminable or accrued. Multi-year commitments may fall outside the ordinary course.

**Push back:** Require a schedule showing term, termination rights and whether each renewal relates to pre- or post-Completion periods. Treat pre-Completion amounts and any non-ordinary-course commitments as debt-like items.

### 15. Mossvale (DD-009): restriction on assignment
The disclosure does not confirm that Mossvale consent is not required by a share sale.

**Push back:** Obtain a clear legal view on whether the restriction is triggered by a change of shareholder, and if so, obtain consent as a condition.

### 16. Title evidence (DD-012)
The Seller relies on the share register showing Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100%. The disclosure itself notes the Buyer has not verified title.

**Push back:** Require an ASIC company extract, a PPSR search, the executed share transfer, confirmation that no options or encumbrances exist, and a title warranty that Harbourglass is the sole legal and beneficial owner, with no third-party interests.

## Part 2: Summary of Recommendations

**Must-have changes before the Buyer can proceed:**
1. Reject general data room disclosure. Require specific, dated disclosure and a bring-down.
2. Delete clause 8.3 and insert an express pro-sandbagging clause.
3. Carve out fraud, fundamental warranties and specific indemnities from all limitations, and reverse the spill-over provision.
4. Title and capacity: full-price cap, outside de minimis and basket, six-year survival.
5. Bluefen consent as a condition precedent, with best-endeavours obligation and long-stop date.
6. Riverlark repaid and discharged at Completion from the price.
7. Ironquay: pre-Completion payment and assignment, plus a special IP indemnity.
8. Privacy incident: forensic investigation and NDB assessment now, plus a specific indemnity.

**Price and structure items:**
9. Treat AUD 420k bonuses (with on-costs), pre-Completion supplier amounts and any unexpired non-ordinary-course commitments as debt-like items.
10. Revise general cap (target 30 to 40%), move to a tipping basket with lower de minimis, and extend general survival to 24 to 36 months.
11. Escrow or holdback (initial discussion point around 10% of price) and/or parent guarantee.
12. Standalone tax indemnity and extended IP warranties.

**Verification and conditions:**
13. Landlord and Mossvale position confirmed in writing.
14. Independent title verification (ASIC, PPSR, share transfer).
15. Confirm whether W&I insurance is in scope, as this changes the cap and retention approach.

**Caveats:** I have worked from the Seller's summaries and the Disclosure Letter, not the full data room documents or the draft SPA. Figures and the percentage ranges above are negotiating proposals, not market-verified positions. The privacy, tax, lease and consumer-law points need confirmation by NSW and Australian specialist counsel before the Buyer relies on them, and the privacy timing point should be checked urgently.
